//: W1: the square kitchen chopper of every Vietnamese kitchen and market meat stall.  Built on dda's kitchen-knife template rather than copied from the cleaver, which carries variants.  A chopper: bash plus cut on a line edge, heavier than dda's cleaver.
description: A heavy, square-bladed kitchen chopper with a round wooden handle, the knife that splits chicken bones and chops pork on the thớt every afternoon.  The spine is thick enough to crack crab shells, and its weight does half the work in a fight.

//: W1: the pig butcher's knife of the wet market, wide in the belly and pointed.  A thrusting knife: stab-led, well balanced, the best butchering blade of the set.
description: A long butcher's knife whose blade swells in the middle like a bầu gourd and narrows to a sharp point.  Market butchers use it to stick and break down pigs before dawn, and it slides between ribs as easily as it did then.

//: W1: the long chopper of Saigon street-gang fights, regularly seized by the police in the 2000s.  Biggest cutting damage of the set, but blade-heavy: uneven balance, no block technique, BRUTAL instead.  Village-forged, so not DURABLE_MELEE.
description: A long, heavy chopping blade that widens toward a squared tip, forged in a country smithy and fitted with a plain wooden grip.  Farmers clear brush with it; in the city it is the weapon the newspapers name when street gangs fight.  It hits terribly hard and recovers slowly.

//: W1: a double-edged dagger.  Fast and accurate (good balance, RAPID), low damage per blow, durable.
description: A straight, double-edged dagger with a brass guard and a cord-wrapped wooden grip, the kind sold under the counter at Chợ Lớn knife stalls and kept in a drawer "for robbers".  It is made for stabbing and nothing else.

//: W1: the Vietnamese hoe is a heavy chopping blade at a right angle to its haft, swung overhead into clay.  Heavier and harder-hitting than dda's hoe, clumsy, no block, BRUTAL.
description: A heavy iron hoe blade set square across a short wooden haft, swung overhead to break the dry-season clay of a vegetable plot.  It is slow to lift and comes down like an axe.

//: W1: the long-handled grass blade of the Mekong delta (phát cỏ bằng phảng), common on the city's farming fringe.  Two-handed sweeping cut: WIDE hits several adjacent targets.
description: The southern grass-cutter: a long, slightly curved blade on a wooden handle as long as your arm, swung low and sideways to mow a canal bank in a few strokes.  Swung at chest height it clears a doorway the same way.

//: W1: the bare pole of a quang gánh.  A sturdy two-handed staff: good block, SWEEP trips.
description: A flat, springy carrying pole split from a thick bamboo, polished by years on a vendor's shoulder, with notches at each end where the basket cords sat.  It bends but does not break, and swung low it takes the legs out from under anything.

//: W1: a plain hollow bamboo staff, the cheapest weapon in the city.  Light, quick and accurate (good balance, RAPID), weak, and FRAGILE_MELEE: hollow bamboo splits.
description: A length of hollow bamboo cut just below a node at each end so it will not split too quickly.  It is light enough to whirl and quick in the hand, but every hard blow cracks it a little more.

//: W1: the training staff (côn) of Vietnamese traditional martial arts, cut from solid-walled tầm vông bamboo.  The best staff: weapon grip, RAPID, SWEEP and WBLOCK_2, durable.
description: A martial-arts staff of tầm vông, the thick-walled bamboo that is nearly solid, oiled dark and wrapped with cord at the grips.  Every võ đường has a rack of them; in trained hands it blocks, sweeps and strikes faster than the eye follows.

//: W1: nunchaku, a schoolboy and gang weapon the police confiscated by the sackful in the 2000s.  RAPID strikes, but uneven balance and no block.
description: Two short hardwood sticks joined by a few links of chain, copied from the kung fu films every video stall rented out.  Spun fast, it raps skulls twice before the first blow lands, and raps your own knuckles just as readily if you have not practised.

//: W1: the delta fish spear (chĩa), used at night for fish, frogs and eels.  Reach stab, and the only weapon here built to be thrown.
description: A fish spear: three barbed iron prongs bound onto the end of a long bamboo shaft.  Delta farmers wade the paddy edges at night with one and a headlamp, stabbing or throwing it at fish and eels.

//: W1: the survivor's polearm, a kitchen blade lashed to bamboo (giáo mác in the old word).  Reach plus a cutting edge, but the lashing works loose: FRAGILE_MELEE.
description: A chopper or long knife lashed into the split end of a bamboo pole and bound tight with cord: the old mác, made again in a hurry.  It keeps the dead at two steps' distance, but every heavy blow loosens the binding.

//: W1: one of the ceremonial weapons (lỗ bộ) that stand on racks in the đình and the Chợ Lớn assembly halls.  Thin tinned iron, never sharpened: heavy, reach, mostly bash, WIDE, and FRAGILE_MELEE.
description: A ceremonial crescent-bladed halberd taken from the weapon rack of a communal house, one of a set that stood guard beside the altar.  The blade is thin tinned iron that was never sharpened and the red-lacquered pole is heavy hardwood.  It was made to be looked at, and it will not last long being used.

//: W1: the southern ná thun, a guava fork with inner-tube rubber.  dda's slingshot mechanism and pebble ammo type, a little more power and range from the tube rubber.
description: A Y-shaped fork of guava wood with two strips of red rubber cut from a bicycle inner tube and a pouch from an old shoe tongue.  Every boy in the hẻm had one for birds and mangoes; loaded with a pebble or a bi, it stings at a few paces and still bruises at six.

//: W1: the Central Highlands crossbow (nỏ Tây Nguyên), rare in the city: hung on a wall by someone from Đắk Lắk, or a working piece bought from a highland maker.  dda crossbow mechanics, lighter and weaker, quicker to span, wider spread; shoots dda bolts and the mod's tên tre.
description: A highland crossbow: a bow of springy cà chít wood set through a carved stock, with a string of twisted bark fibre and a simple wooden trigger peg.  The Ê Đê and M'nông hunt with these.  It shoots thin bamboo bolts quietly, and it takes a strong back to draw.

//: W1: glass marbles (bi ve), a schoolyard game and the best slingshot ammunition in reach.  dda marble stats.
description: Glass marbles with a twist of colour inside, the kind children flick at each other in the dust of a schoolyard.  They fly truer than pebbles from a ná, and they shatter on landing more often than not.

//: W1: steel balls from worn motorbike wheel and steering bearings; a repair shop has a coffee tin of them.  dda ball bearing stats: the hardest-hitting slingshot ammunition.
description: Steel balls knocked out of worn motorbike wheel and steering-head bearings.  Every sidewalk mechanic keeps a tin of them, and every boy with a ná knows to beg for a handful.

//: W1: bamboo bolts for the nỏ (or any crossbow): a sliver of bamboo, fire-hardened point, folded-leaf or paper flights.  dda makeshift wooden bolt mechanics, all bamboo, lighter, breaks more often.
description: A thin crossbow bolt split from bamboo, its point hardened over a fire and its flights a folded scrap of leaf or paper.  Light, quick to make, and lost or broken after a few shots.
